## Overview

Rutulians, also known as the Rutul people or Rutuls, are a Northeast Caucasian ethnic group native to Dagestan and adjacent parts of Azerbaijan. Most live in the Rutulsky District of Dagestan, in settlements associated with the upper reaches of the Samur River; Rutulians also live in Sheki, Kakhi, Sumgait, Ganja, Mingechevir, Baku and other cities in Azerbaijan. According to the 2021 Russian census, there were 34,259 Rutuls in Russia; the exact number in Azerbaijan is unknown. They speak Rutulian, a Northeast Caucasian language, and often have a good command of Azeri and Russian. Their documented livelihoods include cattle breeding, mostly sheep husbandry, farming, gardening, horse breeding, weapons manufacturing, blacksmithing, ceramics and hunting.

## Material culture

### Architecture

The sources describe settlements, fortresses, mosques, minarets, a khanqah and an adit. Archaeological work at the Una settlement examined a fortress on a hill, fortress defenses, a stairway, ancient cemeteries and gravestones. The settlement is described as more than 7000 years old. A road built by local residents during the tsarist era connected Rutul with Akhty and Derbent.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Rutulian inhabitants are described as making weapons, practicing blacksmithing and ceramics, and using tools and materials associated with farming, animal husbandry and hunting. The medieval account of Shinaz mentions the manufacture of armor, chain mail and other types of weaponry. Archaeological finds include openwork bronze bracelets and stone boxes used for burials. The Una settlement contained an adit used to extract copper-bearing ore, with samples showing high concentrations of copper, iron, chromium and nickel.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used mention openwork bronze bracelets found in a burial at Khnov and ancient images of crosses, tamgas and other figures in rock paintings near Ruhudjug.

## Festivals & rituals

The Rutuls adhere to Sunni Islam, while elements of ancient folk beliefs are also described. The sources mention Rutulian *ujag'abyr* sanctuaries, characterized as a type of Caucasian feast. Such sanctuaries occur within general Rutulian traditions and local intra-tukhum practices. One of the oldest feasts mentioned is a 15th-century feast in Hnov.

Sacred groves, mountains, springs, graves and places associated with individual “saints” continued to be worshipped. Fire was considered sacred and revered; the Rutulian peak Tsaylahan is said to mean “place of fire.” The sources also describe legends concerning resistance to Islam. The inhabitants of Ikhrek reportedly resisted its adoption for a long time, while near Arakul the village of Siyakh continued to exist after the appearance of Islam, with inhabitants who professed Judaism.

## Foodways

The sources mention farming, gardening, cattle breeding, horse breeding and transhumance sheep breeding.

A medieval account of Shinaz states that its inhabitants grew a grain called *as-sult* and mountain apples. The sources also mention that the Rutulian society had its own bread and pastures and needed little besides salt. No further foodways are documented in the supplied material.

## Oral tradition & literature

Rutulian oral tradition is represented in the sources by legends concerning the origins of settlements and political communities. One legend states that Rutul was formed from seven small villages, while Shinaz was formed from five. Another concerns the struggle between the Rutulian village of Ikhrek and the now non-existent village of Kharytsa. Legends also describe the siege of Rutul in 1741 by a detachment of Nadir Shah under the command of a Persian khan.

The ancient manuscript *Akhty-name* contains references to Rutul, Jenik and Rufuk and a legend about grandsons of the Arab conqueror Abu Muslim settling in Rutul, Khnov and Shinaz. The medieval author Zakaria al-Qazwini described Shinaz and its inhabitants. Local historical information was recorded in chronicles, tombstones, building stones, mosque walls and minarets.

## Language & religion

Rutulian belongs to the Northeast Caucasian language family. Together with Tsakhur, it forms the Rutul-Tsakhur subgroup of the “Lezgin” or Samur branch of the Nakh-Dagestani family. The sources describe close relationships among Rutul, Tsakhur, Kryz and Budukh, and identify four main Rutulian dialects: Rutul, Shinaz, Ikhrek-Mukhrek and Borchi-Khnov. Rutulian currently has the status of one of the state languages of the Republic of Dagestan.

Before the revolution, Rutulians used the Arabic script. Arabic writing and literature spread with Islam, and Arabic inscriptions in Kufic script occur throughout Rutulian territory. The sources mention inscriptions and religious monuments dating from the 11th through the 13th centuries, including a mosque in Ikhrek dating to the beginning of the 11th century, a mosque inscription in Luchek referring to 745–746, and a tombstone in Khnov dated to 675 AD. Rutuls adhere to Sunni Islam, while elements of earlier beliefs remain associated with sanctuaries, sacred places and fire.
